messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Loss of Control: Lack of control, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Auditory/Threat: Gunshot noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Arjun

Arjun was thirty-two when the conference bombing happened. He had been attending a mental health symposium in Boston, one of the few times in his career as a clinical psychologist that he'd left his practice for professional development. He was sitting in the second row of the main auditorium, listening to a keynote on trauma-informed care, when the sound came—a percussive crack that his brain couldn't immediately categorize. For a fragment of a second, he thought it was part of the presentation, some theatrical effect. Then the ceiling tiles began to fall. People screamed. The noise came again, and again, and in the chaos of bodies pressing toward exits, Arjun found himself pinned against a wall, unable to move, unable to see clearly through the dust, utterly certain that he was going to die in a room full of strangers who couldn't help him and whom he couldn't help.

Five years later, Arjun sits in my office describing a life that has become unrecognizable to him. He is still a psychologist—still sees patients twice a week in a private practice he shares with a colleague—but the man who survived Boston is someone he no longer recognizes. The bombing killed seven people and injured twenty-three others. Arjun walked away physically intact, but he has spent the intervening years slowly withdrawing from the world he once inhabited.

The triggers are specific and relentless. Any loss of control—being stuck in traffic, unable to leave a client session early, dependent on his wife to drive because he no longer trusts his own reflexes—sends him into a state of mounting dread. Nighttime is worse. He lies awake in the dark beside his wife Priya, hypervigilant, listening for sounds that might signal danger. The darkness itself has become a threat; he sleeps with the bedside lamp on, and Priya has learned not to comment on the electricity bill. Most destabilizing is the sound of anything resembling a gunshot—fireworks on the Fourth of July, a car backfiring, even the sharp crack of a wooden spoon against a pot—and when these sounds find him, whether in the street or unexpectedly at home, Arjun's body floods with the certainty that he is back in that auditorium, trapped and powerless.

When these triggers strike, Arjun has developed a repertoire of escape routes. He avoids anything he perceives as stressful: he has stopped attending professional conferences, declined invitations to social gatherings, and increasingly finds reasons not to go out in the evening. His practice has shrunk as he has quietly discouraged new referrals. When the triggers are too immediate to avoid—when a sound pierces through his defenses—he drifts into fantasy, mentally removing himself from the present moment, disappearing into elaborate scenarios where he is safe, in control, untouchable. These dissociative episodes can last minutes or hours. More frequently now, in the early evening when the light begins to fade and his anxiety crests, he pours a drink. Sometimes two. The alcohol softens the edges of his vigilance, quiets the internal alarm that never fully silences. He has also taken to using sleep medication on nights when the dark feels particularly threatening, though he has begun to notice that the medication's effectiveness is waning and he requires increasingly larger doses.

These strategies, which once seemed like survival, have become their own trap. The more Arjun avoids stressful situations, the more the world feels genuinely dangerous—each successful avoidance reinforces his conviction that he cannot trust himself to manage the unexpected. The fantasy escapes, while temporarily relieving his anxiety, leave him feeling more disconnected from his own life; he catches himself mid-session with a client, realizing he has no memory of the last five minutes of what they said. The drinking, which began as occasional relief, has become nightly routine, and with it has come a creeping sense of shame and self-alienation. He is a psychologist who treats others' trauma while medicating his own with alcohol, a contradiction that deepens his sense that the person he has become is fundamentally compromised, unreliable, a shadow of who he was.

This recognition—that he cannot stop bad things from happening, that the world remains inherently dangerous, that he himself has become someone he doesn't recognize—feeds back into his avoidance. The more he believes he is helpless and broken, the more he drinks to quiet that voice. The more he drinks and dissociates, the more he withdraws from his practice and his marriage. Priya has stopped asking him to attend her family gatherings. His colleagues have stopped inviting him to lunch. He has become, in his own mind, a walking liability—and that belief drives him deeper into the very behaviors that confirm it.

It was Priya who finally insisted he seek help. She found him one evening unable to wake from a dissociative episode, his empty glass on the nightstand, the bedroom lamp flickering. She said, quietly, that she was frightened of what he was becoming—and more than that, that she was frightened for him. Arjun came to see me because his wife was right: he no longer recognizes himself, and he is terrified that if he does not find a way out of this cycle, the man he has become will be all that remains.
